title: Command-Line Mode
summary: Chapter 5 explains Command-Line mode and the Ex commands it exposes, opening with a catalog of Ex commands that operate on buffer text and the control-key chords available at the prompt. It shows how to build [range] addresses from line numbers, marks, and patterns, and how to duplicate or move lines with :copy/:t and :move/:m. Later tips cover running Normal mode commands across a range with :normal, repeating Ex commands with @:, tab-completion and wildmode, inserting the word under the cursor with <C-r><C-w>, and recalling history in the command-line window. The final tips cover running shell commands and filtering ranges through external programs, then batching Ex commands in a script and sourcing it across the argument list.

commands.evidence: In Chapter 1, The Vim Way, we saw how the . command can be used to repeat the last change. But the dot command won’t replay changes made from Vim’s command line. Instead, we can repeat the last Ex command by pressing @: (see @:ⓘ).

commands.evidence: At Vim’s command line, the <C-r><C-w> mapping copies the word under the cursor and inserts it at the command-line prompt. We can use this to save ourselves a bit of typing.

concepts.name: Ex commands strike far and wide
concepts.evidence: As a general rule, we could say that Ex commands are long range and have the capacity to modify many lines in a single move. Or to condense that even further: Ex commands strike far and wide.

concepts.name: Visual selection range marks
concepts.evidence: ’< is a mark standing for the first line of the visual selection, while ’> is the last line of the visual selection (see Tip 54, for more about marks). These marks persist even when we leave Visual mode. If you try running :’<,’>p straight from Normal mode, it will always act on the lines that most recently formed a Visual mode selection.

concepts.name: Pattern addresses in a range
concepts.evidence: This looks quite complex, but it follows the usual form for a range: :{start},{end}. The {start} address in this case is the pattern /<html>/, while the {end} address is /<\/html>/. In other words, the range begins on the line containing an opening <html> tag and ends on the line containing the corresponding closing tag.

concepts.evidence: We could shorten the :copy command to only two letters, as :co. Or we can be even more succinct by using the :t command, which is a synonym for :copy. As a mnemonic, you can think of it as copy TO. This table shows a few examples of the :t command in action:

concepts.name: Moving lines with :m
concepts.evidence: We can shorten it to a single letter: :m. Suppose that we want to move the Hardware Store section after the Beauty Parlor section. We could do so using the :move command as shown in Table 8, Moving a Set of Lines with the ‘:m’ Command.

concepts.name: The : register and @: repeat
concepts.evidence: Then we use @: to repeat the command. Note the similarity between this and the method for executing a macro (Play Back a Sequence of Commands by Executing a Macro). Also note that the : register always holds the most recently executed command line (see quote_:ⓘ). After running @: for the first time, we can subsequently repeat it with the @@ command.

concepts.name: Command-line window
concepts.evidence: The command-line window is like a regular Vim buffer, where each line contains an item from our history. With the k and j keys, we can move backward and forward through our history. Or we can use Vim’s search feature to find the line that we’re looking for. When we press the <CR> key, the contents of the current line are executed as an Ex command.

concepts.name: Filtering a range through an external program
concepts.evidence: The :!{cmd} command takes on a different meaning when it’s given a range. The lines specified by [range] are passed as standard input for the {cmd}, and then the output from {cmd} overwrites the original contents of [range]. Or to put it another way, the [range] is filtered through the specified {cmd} (see :range!ⓘ). Vim defines a filter as “a program that accepts text as standard input, changes it in some way, and sends it to standard output.”

concepts.name: Batching Ex commands in a sourced script
concepts.evidence: We can use the :source command to execute the batch.vim script (see sourceⓘ).

problems.evidence: Vim gives special treatment to some commands. For example, both make and grep have wrapper commands. Not only are they easy to execute from inside Vim, but their output is parsed and used to populate the quickfix list. These commands are covered in greater depth in both Chapter 17, Compile Code and Navigate Errors
